summary:
Burn Almanac is a web app that turns NASA's MODIS and VIIRS active-fire hotspots into one consistent fire calendar for any place on Earth, from 2003 to today.

The challenge is that VIIRS sees much finer detail than MODIS. For the same fires it reports about four times as many detections. Joining the two records as they are makes burning look as if it suddenly quadrupled. We fixed this in three steps. First, we merge the small VIIRS pixels into 1 km cells. Second, we calibrate VIIRS against MODIS for every 1° area, separately for day and night, using the years when both flew. Third, we switch to VIIRS from 2022, as the MODIS orbits drift. We tested this by hiding each year in turn and predicting it. The error is 1–2% for the world over a year and about 15% for a region in a single month, compared with about 300% for the raw data.

Users draw an area or pick a region. The app answers in plain words: is this month normal compared with past years, when is the fire season, and what do the next 30 days usually bring? It also has maps, cropland vs. forest fires, CSV downloads, four languages and colour-blind-safe colours.

This matters because fire managers, farmers and researchers need a fire history they can trust.
details:
What it does

Burn Almanac is a web app that answers a simple question for any place on Earth: is the fire activity here normal? It does this with one consistent satellite fire record that runs from 2003 to the present day.

You choose an area in one of four ways: a ready-made region, one of 217 countries, latitude/longitude, or a box drawn on the map. The app then shows:

  • A plain-language verdict for the current period, e.g. "Punjab, 1–14 November 2026: well below normal, 828 fire detections, 15% of what these same 14 days usually see."
  • A fire calendar with every month since 2003 as a coloured cell. Each cell shows its actual number and is marked if it is unusually high or low compared with the long-term median for that month.
  • An outlook: when the local fire season usually starts, peaks and ends, what the next 30 days normally bring, and a live check of the last 7 days pulled straight from NASA FIRMS.
  • A map of where the fires were, on NASA GIBS imagery.
  • What is burning: fires split into cropland, forest and grassland/savanna using NASA's MODIS land cover map.
  • Fire strength: how intense the fires were, from fire radiative power, shown year by year.
  • Downloads: the full data as CSV, the calendar as an image, and a printable report.

How it works

The challenge is that NASA has two generations of fire sensor that count the same fires very differently:

  • MODIS (Terra and Aqua, from 2000) sees the ground in ~1 km pixels.
  • VIIRS (Suomi-NPP from 2012, NOAA-20 from 2018) sees in 375 m pixels and catches smaller, cooler fires.

For the same fires, VIIRS reports about 4.1 times as many detections as MODIS. If you join the two records as they are, burning appears to jump fourfold on the day the sensor changes. Any trend or "is this normal?" question becomes meaningless.

We bring every year into one unit, "what MODIS would have counted", in four steps:

  1. Clean up. We keep only vegetation fires. Gas flares, volcanoes and other static sources are removed, along with low-confidence detections (MODIS confidence below 30; VIIRS low confidence).
  2. Match the pixel size. VIIRS detections are merged into 0.01° (~1 km) cells per day, so one fire isn't counted three or four times by the finer sensor. This alone brings the ratio down from 4.1 to about 2.7.
  3. Calibrate locally. For every 1° area of the planet, with day and night handled separately, we measure how VIIRS compared with MODIS in the years both flew: 2012–2021 for Suomi-NPP and 2018–2021 for NOAA-20. Many 1° cells have too few fires for a stable ratio. For those we use empirical-Bayes shrinkage: a cell's own ratio is pulled toward its 5° region's ratio, which is pulled toward the global ratio, in proportion to how much data each has. Busy areas keep their local behaviour and quiet areas borrow strength from their neighbours.
  4. Join. The record is MODIS up to 2021 and calibrated VIIRS from 2022 onwards, averaged across whichever VIIRS satellites are operating.

Why switch in 2022? We didn't pick the year arbitrarily. We measured the local overpass time of every satellite directly from the fire data. The MODIS satellites are drifting as they near retirement:

  • Aqua's daytime pass moved from 13:33 in 2021 to about 15:24 in 2026.
  • Terra moved from 10:35 to 09:10.
  • Both VIIRS satellites stayed steady at about 13:30.

Fire activity depends strongly on the time of day, so a drifting MODIS stops being comparable with its own past. VIIRS becomes the more reliable base.

Validation. We used leave-one-year-out testing. Each year from 2012 to 2021 was hidden in turn, predicted from the other years, and compared with what MODIS actually recorded.

Scale

Raw VIIRS error

Burn Almanac error

Whole world, one year

~308%

1.0% (Suomi-NPP), 2.0% (NOAA-20)

Whole world, one month

~314%

4.6% / 5.2%

5° region (~500 km), one month

~296%

14.8% / 15.8%

1° area (~100 km), one month

~278%

18.8% / 19.9%

The overall bias is −0.3% for Suomi-NPP and −1.0% for NOAA-20. These figures are shown inside the app, so users know how much to trust a number at the scale they are looking at.

Data pipeline. We processed 26 years of FIRMS archive data, more than 550 million detections. The steps were ingest, aggregation onto a global 0.25° grid, calibration and export. The output is 433 compact binary tiles (about 47 MB in total). The browser loads only the tiles that cover the chosen area, so the app stays fast without a heavy server. Recent 2026 data comes from the FIRMS API, and the record runs to 14 November 2026.

Benefits

  • One honest long-term record. Users get 23+ years of comparable fire history instead of two records that disagree.
  • Answers, not just data. The first thing on screen is a sentence a non-specialist can act on.
  • Fair comparisons for the current month. A half-finished month is never compared with whole months. If today is 14 November, the app compares 1–14 November with 1–14 November of earlier years.
  • Transparent uncertainty. The calibration error is published at each scale, not hidden.
  • Survives satellite loss. Suomi-NPP stopped delivering data on 2 November 2026, and the record continued seamlessly with NOAA-20. The same design will absorb future sensors such as NOAA-21.
  • Free and open. It works in any browser and needs no account. A copy on GitHub Pages works even without a FIRMS key, and visitors can add their own key to get the live features.
  • Exportable. CSV, image and printed report make it easy to put the results into a report, a planning meeting or further analysis.

Intended impact

The users we designed for:

  • Fire and forest managers checking whether this season is unusual and planning staffing for the next month.
  • Agricultural and air-quality agencies tracking crop-residue burning, such as stubble burning in Punjab, which affects the air of millions of people in northern India every October and November.
  • Researchers and students who need a consistent fire time series without first building their own MODIS–VIIRS harmonization.
  • Journalists and the public who want to check claims like "this is the worst fire year ever" against real data.

MODIS is being retired. The long-term fire record that climate, land-use and air-quality work depends on has to move to VIIRS without breaking. Burn Almanac shows one practical, validated way to carry that 20-year baseline into the VIIRS era, and puts the result in the hands of people who don't write code.

Tools, languages and software

Data (all NASA):

  • NASA FIRMS: MODIS Collection 6.1 and VIIRS 375 m (Suomi-NPP, NOAA-20). We used the archive downloads plus the FIRMS area API for recent and live data.
  • NASA GIBS: the Blue Marble shaded-relief basemap, reference features and labels, and the MODIS Combined Land Cover (IGBP) annual product for the cropland/forest/grassland split.
  • One non-NASA source: the Natural Earth country outline, used only as a fallback.

Data pipeline:

  • Python 3.12, DuckDB for fast SQL over hundreds of millions of rows, NumPy, PyArrow/Parquet and Pillow.
  • Bash scripts for the parallel bulk downloads.

Web app:

  • TypeScript, Next.js 16 and React 19.
  • MapLibre GL JS for the map.
  • A custom binary tile format, parsed in the browser.
  • Overpass and Noto Sans Devanagari fonts for the four languages.

Testing:

  • An automated end-to-end test suite (Puppeteer driving Microsoft Edge). It covers area selection, drawing, date ranges, language switching, downloads, printing and the live check: 26 of 26 tests pass on the deployed site.

Hosting:

  • Vercel for the full app, with GitHub Pages as a static backup. The source code is on GitHub.

Hardware:

  • A standard Windows laptop. No special hardware or cloud computing was needed. The whole 26-year archive is processed locally.

How it is creative

  • Local calibration with shrinkage. Most harmonization approaches use one global conversion factor, which is badly wrong locally (31% error at 1° scale in our tests). Our cell → region → globe approach cuts that to about 19% and still behaves well where data are sparse.
  • Measuring orbit drift from the fires themselves. We worked out each satellite's real overpass time from the timestamps of the fire detections. That gave measured evidence for when to switch sensors.
  • The calendar as the interface. Instead of a dashboard full of charts, the core view is a familiar calendar grid. One glance shows the season, the bad years and whether now is unusual.
  • Month-to-date fairness. We store day-of-month data so a partial month is compared like for like. This detail is easy to miss, and getting it wrong produces false "record low" alarms at the start of every month.
  • Built to outlive its satellites. The averaging design handled a real satellite failure (Suomi-NPP) during the challenge without any change to the method.

What our team considered

  • Scientific honesty. We validated before trusting, published the error, and marked partial months clearly. When a fire-type filter is on, we turn off comparisons that would be unfair.
  • Sensor continuity and MODIS retirement. We based the switch year on measured drift, not convenience.
    • The colour ramp runs from dark red to pale yellow and stays readable for colour-blind users.
    • Every cell shows its number, so colour is never the only signal.
    • The calendar works with keyboard arrows.
    • The design is high-contrast and dark, with large type.
  • Language. Plain wording, with no jargon on the main screen. The app is available in English, Hindi, Portuguese and Spanish, covering many of the world's most fire-affected regions.
  • Low bandwidth and cost. We precompute the data into small tiles so the app stays fast on slow connections and costs almost nothing to host.
  • Access without barriers. There is no login. The app works without an API key, and a key is optional for live data.
  • Only open NASA data, so anyone can reproduce and extend the work. The full pipeline is in the repository.
  • Mobile and print. The layout works on phones, and the print view produces a clean report for offline use.
